title: M76 (Little Dumbbell)
caption: The Little Dumbbell Nebula (M76), imaged at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: M76, the Little Dumbbell, shows two distinct features: a bright inner rectangle and very faint outer loops. The rectangle is in fact a ring-shaped torus seen edge-on.

Like most nebulae of this type, these loops were shed as a star of average mass came to the end of its life. More massive stars explode, but this process is much gentler, and it produces the tangled bubbles seen here.

At the heart of the nebula lies a double star, and the upper one is distinctly blue. That hot star is what makes the Little Dumbbell glow, as its energetic light excites the surrounding gas. Its distance is not well known, but most estimates put it between 3000 and 5000 light-years away, which would make the bubble roughly a light-year across. On a dark night, the nebula is a rewarding sight through the 20-inch telescope at Kitt Peak.
scale: M76 is thought to lie between 3000 and 5000 light-years away, making the bubble about a light-year across, according to NOIRLab.

understand.summary: This is a visible-light image taken with a CCD camera at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center's roll-off-roof observatory, using several broadband filters. The packet does not say which colour each filter was assigned.
filters: 438 nm · Optical B (Visitor Center Roll off Roof Observatory Other CCD)

understand.eye: Through the 20-inch telescope the eye can make out both the bright rectangle and the very dim outer loops, but the camera gathers far more of their faint light.

explore: The full-resolution image shows the central double star most clearly. The picture was taken by Adam Block through the Advanced Observing Program at the Kitt Peak Visitor Center in 2014.
